title: this binding: default, implicit, explicit, and arrow functions
hook: In JavaScript, this is not the object where a function was written — it is the object chosen when the function is called. FAANG interviews love the binding matrix because one wrong assumption breaks React handlers, class methods, and callbacks.

blocks.text: **this** is a runtime binding set by the **call site**, not the definition site (except arrow functions and bound functions). The five rules interviewers expect: **default** (strict: undefined; sloppy: global object), **implicit** (`obj.method()` → this is obj), **explicit** (`call/apply/bind`), **new** (`new Fn()` → fresh object), and **arrow** (lexical this from enclosing scope). Class methods use implicit binding when called as `instance.method()`.

entries.plainDefinition: The place in code where a function is invoked — determines this for ordinary functions.
When the function is called as a method on an object, this is that object.
Forcing this with Function.prototype.call, apply, or bind.
Arrow functions do not have their own this — they capture this from the surrounding scope.
entries.example: `const fn = () => this.id;` inside a class field or constructor.

blocks.text: Lost **this** is the top bug in event handlers and array callbacks: `button.addEventListener('click', obj.handleClick)` passes the function without the object — **this** becomes the button or undefined in strict mode. C# instance methods carry **this** implicitly and cannot be "detached" the same way unless you use delegates with explicit targets. TypeScript does not fix runtime **this** — only `this` parameter types and `@typescript-eslint/unbound-method` help at compile time.

blocks.title: Priority when multiple rules apply
blocks.body: new binding beats explicit bind; explicit bind beats implicit; implicit beats default. Arrow functions ignore call-site rules — they use lexical this.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Default binding
items.body: Plain call `fn()` — strict mode: this is undefined. Sloppy mode: global object (window in browsers).

items.title: Implicit binding
items.body: `obj.fn()` — this is obj. Lost if you assign `const f = obj.fn; f()` — only default binding applies.

items.title: Explicit binding
items.body: `fn.call(ctx, a)`, `fn.apply(ctx, [a])`, or `fn.bind(ctx)` — this is ctx (bind creates a new function with fixed this).

items.title: new binding
items.body: `new Constructor()` — this is the new object inside the constructor.

items.title: Arrow / lexical
items.body: Arrow functions inherit this from enclosing function or class field scope — not from how they are called.

diagram.title: this binding decision flow

snippet.label: Default versus implicit binding
snippet.explanation: Line 1: strict mode — default binding is undefined. Line 12: method call — implicit this is api. Line 14–15: extracting method loses implicit binding — classic interview trap.

snippet.label: Explicit bind and call
snippet.explanation: Line 1–3: function uses this.provider. Line 8–9: call/apply set this for one invocation. Line 11–12: bind returns new function with permanent this.

snippet.label: Class methods and arrow class fields
snippet.explanation: Line 6–8: prototype method — detached call loses this. Line 10–12: field arrow closes over construction-time this. Line 19: strict class bodies — default this is undefined.

snippet.label: new binding in constructor
snippet.explanation: Line 1–6: new sets this inside constructor. Line 9: method on instance — implicit works. Line 12–13: per-instance method still loses this when detached.

blocks.title: this in JavaScript versus C#
rows: Always the instance for instance methods
Delegate still carries target unless static
Local functions capture variables, not this rebinding

blocks.title: Passing class method as callback
blocks.body: `setTimeout(this.tick, 1000)` loses this. Fix: `setTimeout(() => this.tick(), 1000)`, `this.tick.bind(this)`, or arrow class field.

blocks.title: Arrow functions as prototype methods
blocks.body: Arrow functions on the prototype are rare and wrong — they close over outer this at definition time, not instance this at call time.

blocks.text: **Soft bind** and **currying** reuse explicit binding patterns. **Class private fields** and **this** interact: `#x` access requires valid instance **this** in class methods. **Proxy** can wrap methods to preserve this. In React class components, autobinding in constructor existed precisely because of implicit binding loss. **Performance**: `bind` allocates a wrapper function — hot paths sometimes use `const self = this` or arrow fields consciously. **Interview tracing**: given `obj.a().b().c()`, determine this at each step from call shape only.

snippet.label: Interview trace — predict output
snippet.explanation: Line 5–7: ordinary function in setTimeout — this is global/undefined, logs undefined. Line 8–10: arrow captures getXLater's this (obj). FAANG loops love this exact pattern.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying this always refers to the object where the function was defined — that is Java/C#, not JS (except arrows). Claiming bind and call are the same — bind returns a new function. Forgetting that strict mode default this is undefined, not window.

interviewTakeaways: this is set by call site: default, implicit, explicit (call/apply/bind), new, or lexical (arrow).
Detaching a method loses implicit binding — const f = obj.m; f() uses default binding.
Arrow functions inherit this from enclosing scope; class field arrows fix React-style callbacks.

60s: Five rules — new beats bind beats implicit beats default; arrows ignore call site. Strict default is undefined. obj.method() binds obj; passing method as callback loses it. Fix with bind, arrow field, or wrapper lambda.
Follow-up: predict this in setTimeout with function versus arrow inside a method.
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'this is the function owner.' Strong: this is chosen at invocation — method call, bind, new, or lexical arrow.
Passing obj.handle as event listener without bind — this becomes the DOM element or undefined.
Using arrow as prototype method expecting instance this — captures outer this instead.

jsTsCorrelations.note: C# instance methods always receive the instance as this — no detached-method trap at runtime.
TS can type this on functions but does not change runtime binding rules.
